## What I did today

Today we learn about **environments** and why the same code can give different
results on two different computers.

The environment we looked at is called
**Pixi**.

## Why do we use environments?

An environment keeps each project separate. 
It also means someone else can rebuild the exact same setup on their own
computer. 

## Installing Pixi

One line in the terminal:

```bash
wget -qO- https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh
```

## Starting a project

Make a new environment for the project:

```bash
pixi init lina_pixi_training -c conda-forge -c bioconda
```

The `-c` parts say where to download software from. 

This creates two files:

- **`pixi.toml`** — the short, readable one. It lists the project name and the
  tools I asked for. This is the file I actually edit.
- **`pixi.lock`** — the long, automatic one. It records the exact versions and
  where they came from. I never edit this by hand, but it is the file that
  makes the setup truly reproducible.

## Quality control

Before analysing sequencing data, we check whether the data is any good. Bad
data gives bad results, no matter how careful the analysis is. Problems come
from contamination, handling mistakes, or the sequencing machine itself.

## What the raw data looks like

Sequencing data comes in **FASTQ** files. Every read takes four lines:

1. The read name, starting with `@`
2. The sequence itself
3. A `+` separator
4. The quality scores, one character per base

The fourth line is the important one. Each character is a score from 0 to 42
saying how sure the machine was about that base. Low scores mean the base
might be wrong.

## FastQC

**FastQC** checks the quality of a whole file at once, so we do not have to
look at millions of reads by hand.

We add it to the Pixi environment, not to the whole computer:

```bash
pixi add fastqc
pixi run fastqc --help
```

## Running it on the cluster

Big files take time, so the work runs on a cluster instead of a laptop. The
cluster uses **SLURM** to decide who runs what and when. We ask for an account,
some time, and a number of cores:

```bash
srun -A project_ID -t 15:00 -n 1 pixi run fastqc
```

For more than one sample it is easier to put the same settings into a small
script and submit it:

```bash
sbatch fastqc.sh
```

The script is also a record of exactly what was run, which is the reproducible
part.

## MultiQC

One report per sample adds up quickly. **MultiQC** collects them all into a
single report, so the whole dataset can be checked in one place.

## Keeping the session alive

If the connection to the cluster drops, the job dies with it. `screen` keeps
it running:

```bash
screen -S fastqc     # start a session
# Ctrl + a, then d   # leave it running
screen -r fastqc     # come back to it later
```
